name: 4-n-Butylresorcinol

lead: 4-n-Butylresorcinol (butylresorcinol, rucinol) is a lab-made ingredient in serums and creams that fades melasma and age spots for a clearer, more even skin tone.

It inhibits tyrosinase and has been reported to affect tyrosinase-related protein-1, reducing melanin production in cells. It has been tested in several small randomized human trials, including split-face and vehicle-controlled designs, which reported pigment improvement versus vehicle. The trials are small and short, and head-to-head comparisons with other agents are limited.

paras: It is applied as a serum or cream to pigmented areas, usually with daily sunscreen, and trial results are assessed over weeks.
Reports describe minimal irritation at studied concentrations. Regulation varies by country.

angle.text: Used in serums and creams to fade melasma and age spots for a more even tone. It inhibits tyrosinase, so less melanin forms. Several small randomized trials have reported improvement versus vehicle.

lead: 4-n-Butylresorcinol (also called butylresorcinol or rucinol) is a synthetic resorcinol derivative found in serums and creams aimed at dark spots, melasma, age spots and uneven skin tone. People use it to fade patches of excess pigment so the complexion looks more even and bright, usually applied twice daily and paired with daily sunscreen [1][2][3].

It works by blocking tyrosinase, the enzyme at the rate-limiting step of melanin production, and has also been reported to act on tyrosinase-related protein-1 [2][4]. A 2013 comparison of well-known lightening ingredients in a human tyrosinase assay and a reconstructed skin model reported that 4-n-butylresorcinol had a much lower inhibitory concentration than hydroquinone, arbutin or kojic acid [5].

Several small human studies have examined it. Randomized split-face trials in melasma used concentrations of 0.1% and 0.3% over 8 to 12 weeks and reported lower pigment scores or melanin index on the treated side than on the vehicle side [1][4][6]. An open-label study in India, a trial of a microneedle patch and a pilot study of a multi-ingredient serum have reported improvement as well [7][8][9].
infobox: 0.1% to 0.3% in cream, serum or microneedle patch [1][4][7]
Reported as a hypopigmenting agent from about 1995 [6]
Cosmetic ingredient in Europe; quasi-drug whitening agent in Japan (per secondary summary) [17]

paras: The main use is topical fading of hyperpigmentation: melasma on the cheeks, forehead and upper lip, age spots (solar lentigines) on the face and forearms, and dullness from uneven pigment. Products pair it with other brightening ingredients such as niacinamide, vitamin C or glycolic acid, and with broad-spectrum sunscreen, which dermatology reviews describe as a cornerstone of pigment care [3][9][10].

Some formulations encapsulate the ingredient in liposomes to improve stability and skin penetration, and dissolving microneedle patches have been studied as a way to deliver more of it to the pigment-producing layer [4][8][11].

Melasma is a common acquired condition of tan to grey-brown facial patches, more frequent in women and in people with darker skin or strong sun exposure, linked to sunlight, hormonal factors and genetics. It tends to be chronic and to return, which is one reason many topical agents are studied [3][10][12]. A 2019 systematic review of randomized trials covered 35 trials across more than 20 topical agents including 4-n-butylresorcinol; it gave its strongest recommendations to cysteamine, triple combination cream and tranexamic acid [13]. Expert reviews have listed butylresorcinol among the alternatives to hydroquinone that are being tested in clinical trials [3][12].

Melanin is produced by melanocytes through a chain of reactions in which tyrosinase is the rate-limiting enzyme. A 2005 study in a mouse melanocyte line found that 4-n-butylresorcinol reduced melanin synthesis in a concentration-dependent way and inhibited tyrosinase activity [2]. Reviews and trial reports describe additional inhibition of tyrosinase-related protein-1, which is involved in eumelanin synthesis and is more highly expressed in melasma skin [1][4][3][6].

The 2013 comparison reported that 4-n-butylresorcinol inhibited human tyrosinase with an IC50 of about 21 micromolar, versus roughly 500 micromolar for kojic acid and the millimolar range for arbutin and hydroquinone. In reconstructed pigmented skin, 4-n-butylresorcinol had an IC50 of about 13.5 micromolar and was the most potent of the compounds tested [5]. A 2017 cell study reported that it also promoted proteolytic degradation of tyrosinase in B16F10 melanoma cells [14]. A 2015 screening method was developed to distinguish tyrosinase-inhibiting whitening phenols from phenols that can induce leukoderma through formation of reactive quinones [15].

The first widely cited trial was published in 2007: a single-centre, double-blind, vehicle-controlled split-face study in which 32 women with melasma applied 0.3% rucinol serum to one half of the face and vehicle to the other half twice daily for 12 weeks, with SPF 60 sunscreen daily. Twenty-eight completed phase 1. The clinical pigmentation score was significantly lower on rucinol-treated skin than on vehicle-treated skin (P = 0.027), and in an optional 3-month open-label phase the formerly vehicle-treated side also improved [1].

A 2010 Korean split-face trial enrolled 20 melasma patients to 0.1% cream or vehicle twice daily for 8 weeks; the melanin index on the treated side was significantly lower than on the vehicle side at 4 weeks (p=0.006) and 8 weeks (p<0.0005), with mild, transient adverse reactions [6]. A second 2010 split-face trial of liposome-encapsulated 0.1% cream enrolled 23 patients over 8 weeks and reported a lower melanin index on the treated side at 8 weeks (P = 0.043), no adverse reactions, and subjective efficacy in more than 60% of patients [4].

In an open-label, single-arm Indian multicentre study, 52 people with melasma applied 0.3% cream twice daily for 8 weeks; mean modified MASI scores fell from 14.73 at baseline to 11.09 at week 4 and 6.48 at week 8, with no adverse reactions reported [7]. A 2020 study of 21 women using a cream combining liposomal 4-n-butylresorcinol with resveratrol for 4 weeks reported lower lesional melanin index and improved investigator scores from week 2 [9]. A 2022 open-label pilot in 12 women with melasma tested a serum combining several actives, including 4-n-butylresorcinol, with an SPF50+ sunscreen for 12 weeks and reported improvement on clinical and confocal-microscopy measures; its authors called for larger controlled studies [16].

The 2013 paper also reported two in vivo studies on forearm age spots: in the first, treated spots visibly faded within 8 weeks while vehicle-treated spots did not, and in the second 4-butylresorcinol outperformed 4-hexylresorcinol and 4-phenylethylresorcinol [5]. A 2016 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 45 subjects tested a dissolving microneedle patch containing 4-n-butylresorcinol over 8 weeks; the active patch was reported to be more than twice as effective as the control patch on melanin index and typology angle, and irritation and sensitization tests in 31 and 50 volunteers found it safe [8].

Trial sizes are small (12 to 52 participants), durations are 4 to 12 weeks, and the studies measured melanin index, MASI or investigator scores. Head-to-head trials against hydroquinone or other leading agents are limited [13][12].

Adverse events in the trials were described as mild and transient or absent, and the microneedle patch passed primary irritation, cumulative irritation and sensitization testing [4][6][7][8]. The Indian study noted that skin there is considered more prone to irritation with hypopigmenting agents and reported no adverse reactions at 0.3% [7].

An AI-generated encyclopedia summary states that the compound is permitted as a cosmetic ingredient in the EU and is a quasi-drug whitening agent in Japan; that page can contain errors, and the regulatory details are best checked against regulator sources [17].

4-n-Butylresorcinol was described as a hypopigmenting agent in the mid-1990s, with the Korean trial authors dating its introduction to 1995 [6]. Laboratory characterisation of its effect on melanin synthesis followed in 2005 [2], the first widely cited randomized melasma trial of a rucinol serum appeared in 2007 [1], and further formulation work on liposomes, microneedle patches and resveratrol combinations followed [4][8][9].

Studies have examined dissolving microneedle patches used alone or over serum-treated skin to increase delivery of 4-n-butylresorcinol, and nanoliposome formulations to improve stability and penetration [8][11][18].
